I. INTRODUCTION
Francis Fahy (Fahy), an attorney representing himself in this case, filed an appeal
from an order declaring him a vexatious litigant and dismissing his malpractice complaint
against attorney Steven Pisano (Pisano). On August 15, 2001, this court filed an order
striking Fahy’s opening brief and appellant’s appendix from this record. We instructed
the clerk of this court to return those documents to Fahy for corrections in compliance
with the California Rules of Court and we expressly advised that failure to file a
corrected brief would result in dismissal of this appeal. Pursuant to our August 15, 2001, ;
order, we now dismiss this appeal. In addition, we impose monetary sanctions against
Fahy. |
ll. FACTS AND PROCEDURAL BACKROUND
A. Proceedings In the Lower Court .
On September 20, 2000, Fahy filed a complaint against Pisano purporting to allege
causes of action for attorney malpractice, negligence, fraud, breach of fiduciary duty and
emotional distress. Both Fahy and Pisano represented themselves during the proceedings
in the lower court. .
1
 
On February 21, 2001, the trial court filed an order declaring Fahy to be a
vexatious litigant within the meaning of Code of Civil Procedure sections 391 et seq.
The court imposed a pre-filing order on Fahy prohibiting him from filing any new
litigation in pro per without first obtaining leave of the presiding judge of the court where
the litigation was proposed to be filed. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 391.7, subd. (a).) In
addition, the court concluded it was not reasonably likely that Fahy would prevail on his
current complaint against Pisano and, therefore, ordered Fahy to furnish security in the
amount of $15,000 in order to proceed with this case. (See Code Civ. Proc., § 391.3.)
On March 23, 2001, the trial court filed an order dismissing Fahy’s action against Pisano
pursuant to section 391.4 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that Fahy failed to
furnish the security required by the court’s February 21, 2001, order.
B. The Appeal
On March 19, 2001, before the lower court dismissed Fahy’s case, Fahy filed a
notice of appeal in the superior court. Fahy appealed from all orders, final rulings and
judgments of the superior court and elected to proceed pursuant to section 5.1 of the Code
of Civil Procedure [sic]. On March 22, 2001, Fahy filed an amended notice of appeal and
notice to proceed pursuant to section 5.1 of the Code of Civil Procedure [sic]. Both the
notice of appeal and the amended notice of appeal were lodged with this court on March
26, 2001.
On July 9, 2001, Fahy filed an appellant’s opening brief and an appellant’s
appendix. On July 24, 2001, Pisano filed a motion to strike Fahy’s opening brief and
appellant’s appendix on the ground that both violated the California Rules of Court.’
On August 15, 2001, this court filed the following order: “Respondent’s motion to
strike appellant’s appendix and appellant’s opening brief filed with this court on July 9,
All rule references are to the California Rules of Court.
Several rules relevant to this appeal were revised and/or renumbered effective
January 1, 2002. With the exception of Fahy’s reply brief, all of the documents Fahy
filed in this court were filed before January 1, 2002, and, therefore, were not subject to
requirements which became effective on that date,
2
 
2001 is granted. The Clerk of this court is directed to return the appellant’s opening brief
and appendix to appellant for corrections in compliance with the California Rules of
Court, specifically rules 5.1, 13, 15(a) and 46. [%{] Appellant shall submit an original and |
4 copies of the corrected opening brief and an original of the appendix to this court for
filing within 30 days from the date of this order. Failure to file the corrected brief will
result in dismissal pursuant to rule 17{a).”
. . On September 12, 2001, Fahy filed another appellant’s appendix and appellant’s |
opening brief. On January 15, 2002, Pisano, who is not representing himself on appeal,
filed a 49-page respondent’s brief and a 174-page respondent’s appendix. In his brief,
Pisano responded to Fahy’s substantive challenges to the lower court’s rulings. Pisano
also requested that sanctions be imposed against Fahy pursuant to section 907 of the
Code of Civil Procedure and rule 26(e) on the ground that Fahy’s appeal is frivolous and
that Fahy’s opening brief and appellant’s appendix unreasonably violate the rules of
court.
- Pisano filed two declarations in support of his request that Fahy pay his attorneys’
fees as sanctions. Pisano’s appellate counsel, James Moneer, filed a declaration
requesting he be awarded a total of $64,915.00 which includes a lodestar with multiplier
to reflect his claimed expertise. In addition, Pisano has filed his own declaration seeking
. an additional award of $10,055.87 for legal work he has performed on his own behalf.
Fahy filed a reply brief on February 4, 2002. In the text of his reply brief, Fahy
- “request[ed]” leave to supplement his appellant’s appendix with approximately 50 pages
of documents he attached to his reply brief. On February 13, 2002, Fahy filed an “Errata
_ Sheet” with respect to his reply brief. This document contains a declaration by Fahy in
which he stated that he was caring for a sick friend while preparing his reply brief and
those efforts resulted in a “great number of typographical errors” in the reply brief. Fahy
stated the errors resulted from “excusable neglect” and asked us to consider correcting
the numerous (more than 20) errors.
| 3
 
ll. DISCUSSION
We need not address the merits of Fahy’s appeal because, as explained herein, we
conclude that this appeal must be dismissed and that monetary sanctions must be imposed
against Fahy.
A. Fahy’s Appendix and Briefs Violate The Rules of Court
1, The Appellant’s Appendix
As noted above, Fahy elected to proceed under the provisions of rule 5.1 by
submitting an appellant’s appendix rather than having the superior court prepare a clerk’s
. transcript. Fahy’s appendix violates several provisions of the version of rule 5.1 that was
in effect when his appendix was filed.
Former rule 3.1 requires that the notice of appeal be included in the appellant’s
appendix. (Former rule 5.1(b)(1); former rule 5(d)(1).} In the present case, the
appellant’s appendix does not contain a copy of the notice of appeal or the amended
notice of appeal. Instead, Fahy has included a copy of a so-called second amended notice
of appeal. There is no evidence either on the face of that document or in this court’s
records that a second amended notice of appeal was filed in this case.
The documents that may be included in the appellant’s appendix must have been
filed or lodged with the clerk of the superior court. (Former rule 5.1 (b)(2); former rule
5(d)}; former rule 4.5; see also Deers v. Golden Gate Bridge, Etc. Dist. (1979) 23 Cal.3d
180, 184.) Further, copies of the superior court documents must be conformed to show
the date of filing in the trial court if the clerk’s date stamp does not appear on them.
(Former rule 5.1(¢)(1).) Indeed, the attorney who files an appendix represents to the
court that the appendix “consists of true and correct copies of the papers in the superior
court file.” (Former rule 5.1(i)(1).) Fahy’s appendix violates all three of these
provisions. Many documents in the appeHant’s appendix bear no clerk’s date stamp and
have not been conformed to show the date of filing. Some documents contain court
stamps from other cases, some documents are incomplete and some relate to other
unidentified cases. We cannot ascertain whether most of the documents contained in the
appellant’s appendix were part of the record below.
. 4 |
 
The appellant’s appendix must contain documents from the lower court file that
“are essential to the proper consideration of the issues, including such documents as the
appellant should reasonably assume will be relied upon by the respondent in meeting the
issues raised.” (Former rule 5.1(b)(2); former rule 5(d).) “It is appellant’s responsibility
to include all essential documents in the appellant’s appendix -- even those that might be
relied on by respondent. [Citation.]” (Eisenberg, et al., Cal. Practice Guide: Civil
Appeals and Writs (The Rutter Group 2001) { 4:199, p. 4-44.) Further, a court may
impose monetary sanctions when the appellant’s appendix is “so inadequate that justice
cannot be done without requiring inclusion of documents in the respondent’s appendix
which should have been in the appellant’s appendix ... .” (Former rule 5.1(i)(2).)
In the present case, many of the documents we would need in order to understand
the substantive issues and procedural history of this case were not included in the
appellant’s appendix but are found in the respondent’s appendix. These documents
include: (1) the complaint, (2) Pisano’s motion for an order declaring Fahy to be a
vexatious litigant, (3) the pleadings and evidence Pisano filed in support of that motion,
and (4) Pisano’s motion for an order dismissing this case and the pleadings and evidence
filed in support of that motion.’ .
The contents of the appellant’s appendix must be arranged in chronological order.
_ (Former rule 5.1(c)(1); former rule 9(d).) The documents in Fahy’s appendix are not
arranged in chronological order or in any other order. The appendix is confusing and
disorganized.
; Although an appellant is not required to arrange for preparation of a reporter’s |
transcript in every case, an appellant should make such arrangements when consideration
of the oral proceedings is necessary to address the issues on appeal. (Former rule 4(a).)
In the present case, Fahy did not request that a reporter’s transcript be prepared. Without
a transcript of the crucial hearings that led to dismissal of this case, we have serious
doubts as to whether we could properly review the trial court’s findings that Fahy is a
vexatious litigant and that he would not likely succeed on his claims against Pisano in
this case.
5
 
Documents may not be incorporated by reference into an appellant’s appendix
except for the record of (1) another case pending before the same appellate court or (2) a
prior appeal in the same case. (Former rule 5.1 (c)(3).) Fahy’s opening brief contains a
completely incoherent section entitled “Regarding the Appendix on Appeal” in which
Fahy improperly purports to incorporate by reference into his appendix seven “cases,
along with evidence included in them.”
2. Fahy’s Opening Brief
Fahy filed a second opening brief on September 12, 2001. We cannot directly
compare this document to the first brief Fahy filed because the Jatter was stricken from
our record. However, this second brief fails to comply with several provisions of the
rules of court that were in effect when it was filed.
Former rule 13 requires that an appellant’s opening brief contain, among other
things, a concise but complete “statement of the case” which sets forth the nature of the
action, the relief sought, a summary of the material facts and the judgment or ruling of
the superior court and which is “accurate and confined to matters in the record on
appeal,” Fahy’s statement of the case is neither concise nor complete. Instead, it is a
confusing morass of factual allegations pertaining to numerous prior lawsuits Fahy has
filed. Furthermore, it is impossible for us to determine which if any of these matters were
presented to the lower court.
Former rule 15(a) requires that “[t]he statement of any matter in the record shall be
supported by appropriate reference to the record.” In our August 15, 2001 order, we
expressly instructed Fahy. to file a brief that complied with this rule because the first
opening brief he filed did not contain any record citations at all. We are very disturbed to
find that Fahy’s second opening brief does not contain a single reference to the record.
Oddly, some of Fahy’s factual allegations are followed by “(AA __).” But, the opening
brief does not contain a single page reference to the appellant’s appendix.
Former rule 15(b)(6)(iii) requires that the California State Bar membership
number of the attorney filmg the appellant’s opening brief be stated on the cover of the
brief. Fahy did not provide his state bar number on any of his briefs.
6
 
Rule 977 states that, with exceptions not relevant here, an opinion of the court of
appeal that is not certified for publication or ordered published “shall not be cited or
relied on by a court or a party in any other action or proceeding ....” Fahy’s opening
brief contains a lengthy and completely incoherent discussion of Randall v. Scovis
notwithstanding the fact that our Supreme Court ordered that decision depublished.
(Randall v. Scovis (2001) 105 Cal.Rptr.2d 32, previously published at 87 Cal.App.4th
631.)
3. Fahy’s Reply Brief
Fahy filed his reply brief on February 4, 2002. Thus, this brief is subject to the
rules as amended January 1, 2002.
Rule 14(a)(1)(C) requires that a brief “support any reference to a matter in the
record by a citation to the record.” Although some of the factual assertions in Fahy’s
reply brief are followed by references to the record, many such assertions are not.
Rule 14(d) states that a party may attach 10 pages of exhibits or other material
from the appellate record to his brief. An attachment exceeding 10 pages in length
requires an application to the court and a showing of good cause. Without submitting an
application or even attempting to show good cause, Fahy attached approximately 50
pages of documents to his reply brief and thereby attempted to supplement his appellant’s
appendix. It is not clear whether any of those documents were part of the record in the
lower court.
Rule 46, which was not affected by the 2002 rule revisions, states: “No record,
brief, or other paper or document which fails to conform to the requirements of these
rules shall be filed by the clerk of the reviewing court.” Fahy’s reply brief like his
opening brief, failed to conform to the requirements of the rules of court. .
B. Dismissal of the Appeal is Proper oe
Filing an appellant’s appendix that provides no means of assuring the accuracy of
the record on appeal is a ground for dismissal of the appeal. (/n re Marriage of Green
(1984) 159 Cal. App.3d 1163 (Green).) In Green, the appellant filed a combined opening
brief and appellant’s appendix that “failed to contain the notice of appeal, conformed .
7 .
 
copies and required indices and numbering pages.” Division Three of this court struck
the document and provided appellant another opportunity to comply with former rule 5.1.
Upon failure to comply, the court dismissed the appeal and imposed monetary sanctions.
(id. at p. 1164.) The court reasoned that the purpose of former rule 5.1(i} was to assure
the accuracy of the record on appeal. It dismissed the appeal pursuant to the provision
that “*[w]illful or grossly negligent filing of an appendix containing nonconforming
copies is an unlawful interference with the proceedings of the reviewing court, and
subjects the counsel filing the brief, and the party represented, to monetary and other
appropriate sanctions.” (/d. at p. 1165, fn. 4, italics omitted, quoting former rule
5.1(i)(1).)
In the present case, we struck Fahy’s original appellant’s appendix and provided
him another opportunity to comply with the rules. The appendix Fahy subsequently filed
fails to substantially comply with the rules, Among other things, we simply cannot
determine whether most of the documents included in the appendix were part of the lower
court record. Fahy is both the party and the attorney responsible for the willful or grossly
negligent filing of the appellant’s appendix in this case. Dismissal of the appeal is,
therefore, an appropriate sanction.
Furthermore, this court has inherent power to dismiss an appeal when an appellant
has failed to substantially comply with the rules of court after his initial filmgs were
stricken for noncompliance with the rules. (Berger v. Godden (1985) 163 Cal.App.3d
1113, 1117-1119 (Berger); cf. Green supra, 159 Cal.App.3d at pp. 1164-1 165.) In
Berger, this court struck the opening brief of an appellant who, like Fahy, failed to
comply with rules 13 and 15. We gave the Berger appellant 30 days to file a new brief.
(Berger, supra, 163 Cal.App.3d at p. 1116.) After appellant filed a second brief that
consisted of three pages and contained no citations to the record or to any legal authority,
we dismissed the appeal. One of three independent grounds upon which we based our
decision was “the failure of appellant to file a brief in conformity with the rules after his
initial brief was stricken for noncompliance with the rules ....” (Id. at p. 1117.)
8
 
In the present case Fahy filed both an opening brief and an appellant’s appendix
that failed to substantially comply with the rules of court. We gave Fahy the opportunity
to file another brief and appendix and warned him that failure to comply with the rules
would result in dismissal of his appeal. Fahy ignored our warning and directly violated
our explicit order to comply with the rules. As outlined above, the appellant's appendix
and opening brief violate several rules of court including former rules 5.1, 13, 15(a) and
rule 46, all of which we expressly identified in our August 15, 2001, order. Fahy’s
egregious failure to comply with this court’s order is an independent pround for
dismissing this appeal.
C. Monetary Sanctions
In his respondent’s brief, Pisano requests that we order Fahy to pay Pisano’s
attorneys fees as a sanction pursuant to rule 26(e) and section 907 of the Code of Civil
Procedure (section 907). There are several problems with Pisano’s request.
Rule 26(e) states, in part: “A party seeking monetary sanctions on the ground the |
appeal is frivolous or taken solely for purposes of delay, or for an unreasonable infraction
. of the rules governing appeals, shall serve and file a motion under rule 41... .” “The
prescribed motion procedure is mandatory ... . Consequently, past practice under which
appellate sanctions were commonly sought in respondent’s brief is no longer permissible.
[Citations.]” (Eisenberg, et al., Cal. Practice Guide, supra, J 11:126, p. 11-45.) Here, |
Pisano did not file a rule 41 motion.
Section 907 provides that “[wJhen it appears to the reviewing court that the appeal
was frivolous or taken solely for delay, it may add to the costs on appeal such damages as
. may be just.” Thus both section 907 and rule 26 authorize imposing monetary sanctions
for filing a frivolous appeal. Pisano maintains the present appeal is frivolous and that
requiring Fahy to pay his attorneys fees is an appropriate sanction under these tules. (See
Pierotti v. Torian (2000) 81 Cal.App.4th 17, 29; Kurokawa v. Blum (1988) 199
Cal.App.3d 976.) The problem with this argument is that addressing it would require us
to analyze Fahy’s substantive arguments. Such an analysis simply is not appropriate in
. 9
 
light of our conclusion that this appeal should be dismissed because of Fahy’s many
violations of the rules of court and of our August 15, 2001, order.
Indeed, we are concerned by Pisano’s decision to incur significant expense by
responding to Fahy’s substantive arguments in light of Fahy’s complete failure to comply
with our August 15, 2001, order and the rules of court. The more reasonable course
would have been to file another motion strike or a motion to dismiss this appeal. Further,
our concern about Pisano’s motivation significantly increased after we reviewed the
declarations he filed in support of his request for sanctions. The fees Pisano seeks are not
even limited to the time appellate counsel (unreasonably in our view) spent responding to
Fahy’s opening brief. Pisano also seeks additional significant sums to reflect his
counsel’s claimed expertise. And, he also seeks payment for time he personally spent on
this case. These bold requests do not sit well with us.
In any event, this court has inherent authority to impose monetary sanctions on
Fahy pursuant to our own motion for Fahy’s violations of the rules of court. (Rule
26(a)(2); former rule 5.1(i); rule 5.1(f); Bryan v. Bank of America (2001) 86 Cal.App.4th
185, 192-199 [and authority discussed therein]; Alicia T. v. County of Los Angeles (1990) |
222 Cal.App.3d 869, 884-886.) On March 27, 2002, we gave Fahy notice of our intent to
impose monetary sanctions. (See rule 26(¢).) We now conclude that an appropriate
monetary sanction consists of two components, an amount sufficient to compensate
. Pisano for attorney time reasonably spent with respect to this appea] and an amount
sufficient to compensate this court for the time wasted processing this appeal.
In fixing the amount of sanctions Fahy should pay Pisano we may consider “the
amount of respondent’s attorney fees on appeal; the amount of the judgment against.
appellant; the degree of objective frivolousness and delay; and the need for
discouragement of like conduct in the future.” (Pierotti v. Torian, supra, 81 Cal.App.4th
at pp. 33-34.) Here, there is no monetary judgment against Fahy and we have declined to
spend the additional time necessary to determine whether and how frivolous this appeal
may be. However, we clearly do wish to discourage like conduct by Fahy in the future
and thus we think it appropriate to make him pay for the amount of attorney time
10
 
reasonably spent by Pisano’s counsel in this case. After reviewing the declaration and
time records of Pisano’s appellate attorney, James Moneer, we conclude that $8,500
payable to Pisano is a reasonable sanction to both compensate Pisano for time reasonably ;
spent and to deter Fahy from engaging in conduct like that displayed mm the present case.”
Fahy’s conduct during this appeal has been costly not just to Pisano. “‘In the same
vein, the appellate system and the taxpayers of this state are damaged by what amounts to
a waste of this court’s time and resources. [Citations.]’” (Pierotti v. Torian, supra, 81
Cal.App.4th at p. 35.) A recent conservative estimate of the cost to the state of
processing an average civil appeal is $6,000. (/d. at p. 36.) We find that amount, payable
to the clerk of this court, is an appropriate additional sanction in this case. |
| | IV. DISPOSTION
This appeal is dismissed and Fahy is ordered to pay monetary sanctions in the
amount of $8,500 to Pisano and $6,000 to the clerk of this court. The clerk is. directed to
deposit said sum in the general fund. All sanctions shall be paid no later that 15 days
after the date the remittitur is filed. The clerk is further directed to preclude Fahy from
filing any documents in this court unless and until the monetary sanctions are paid.
Pisano is awarded his costs on appeal.
5 This amount reflects 34 hours of attorney work at a rate of $250 per hour. Our
estimate of the time Mr. Moneer reasonably spent on this case excludes time spent
attempting to establish Moneer’s alleged expertise and time spent responding to the
substantive issues relating to this appeal. The $250 hourly rate is based on Mr. Moneer’s
representation that he was awarded fees at this rate in a routine SLAPP case that did not
require “expert” services. None of the expertise that Mr. Moneer claims to have was
needed to recognize that Fahy’s egregious failure to comply with the rules of court and
this court’s order warranted a second motion to strike and/or a motion to dismiss of this
appeal.
11
 
Haerle, J.
We concur:
